extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in philosophy of humor, aesthetics, and literary theory; researchers working on incongruity accounts of humour
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical defence and refinement of Noël Carroll’s formal incongruity theory of humour, including a proposed 'pertinence condition' and worked literary examples to test and sharpen theoretical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of an incongruity is necessary for comic amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: The key claim of incongruity theory: the perception of an incongruity is necessary for comic amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the necessary condition targeted by various criticisms (counterexamples to necessity such as caricatures, imitations, and repetition). The article treats this as the starting point for evaluating formal definitions of incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carroll's formal notion of incongruity (comparative/discordant relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carroll describes incongruity as 'a comparative notion. It presupposes that something is discordant with something else. With respect to the comic amusement, that something else is how the world is or should be.' Incongruity is a violation of general norms and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a minimal/formal definition: identify a pattern of norms or expectations (how the world is/should be) and an element that infringes them. The article shows how this definition can be informative by applying it to literary passages to capture similarities and differences in comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carroll's jointly sufficient conditions for comic amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Carroll supplements the necessary incongruity condition with additional jointly sufficient conditions intended to exclude non-comic incongruities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taken together these conditions are meant to ensure that an identified incongruity will produce comic amusement rather than other attitudes (e.g., puzzlement, fear). They are presented as a package that together with the necessary condition are jointly sufficient for comic amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived as non-threatening or otherwise non-anxiety-producing
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Carroll’s sufficiency conditions: the incongruity must be perceived as non-threatening or otherwise not anxiety producing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition is used to exclude horror or disturbing incongruities (example: a grotesque or terrifying breach of expectation would fail this condition and not be comic). The article notes some counterexamples where this condition alone does not discriminate (e.g., some surrealist works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity should not be perceived as 'annoying'
rubrics_metrics.description: Carroll requires that the incongruity should not be perceived as annoying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is another restriction among the sufficiency conditions to filter out non-comic reactions. The article treats it as part of the cluster of experiential constraints Carroll proposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Should not 'enlist genuine problem-solving attitudes'
rubrics_metrics.description: Carroll’s account excludes incongruities that require a problem-solving attitude (e.g., puzzles or riddles where the enjoyment derives from finding a solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition separates comic incongruities from puzzle-driven enjoyment: if the appropriate response is to solve or dispel the incongruity, it is not the kind that yields comic amusement under Carroll’s account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Should 'give rise to the enjoyment of precisely the pertinent incongruity' and 'to an experience of levity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Carroll requires that the response be enjoyment specifically of the incongruity in question and that it gives rise to levity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These experiential criteria aim to distinguish comic appreciation from aesthetic appreciation or other reactions. The article uses these to show where Carroll’s conditions succeed and where they leave room for refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pertinence condition (Bariselli's amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed pertinence condition requires that the elements generating an incongruity are part of the same context; the norms/expectations violated must be pertinent to the same context as the violating element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This amendment aims to block 'shoehorning' (fabricating an incongruity by appealing to norms irrelevant to the relevant context). Examples: distinguishes The Three Stooges gags (everyday norms about inanimate objects are pertinent, producing comedy) from Beauty and the Beast (fantasy world where those norms are not pertinent, producing fantastical enjoyment rather than comic amusement); distinguishes Beckett passages where violated norms are pertinent (comic) from Ill Seen Ill Said where they're not (estrangement). The pertinence condition preserves flexibility about which norms count while regulating relevance to the context and makes the theory falsifiable (a counterexample would be a comic instance that depends on violation of non-pertinent rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shoehorning / requirement of falsifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism (shoehorning): a notion of incongruity that lets one find some incongruity for any putative example risks unfalsifiability; a viable theory must avoid being trivially adaptable to any case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that the pertinence condition addresses this desideratum by constraining which incongruities count as explanatory. It also considers (and rejects as insufficient) other restrictions that attempt to prevent shoehorning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cochrane's restrictive norm-criterion (rule-based and intentional norms only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tom Cochrane's amendment: comic amusement requires violation of rule-based norms ('how something ought to be') and norms related to intentional actions or attitudes, excluding statistical, teleological, or purely physical norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents Cochrane’s proposal as a response to shoehorning but argues it is too restrictive (fails to account for cases like Wile E. Coyote, Gogol’s The Nose, and comedic uses of statistical/repetition-based norms such as running gags). Cochrane's criterion is discussed as an alternative constraint the literature has proposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical method: identify which norms/expectations are breached to capture comedic similarity and difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological guidance: to analyse comic instances, indicate the pattern(s) of norms or expectations breached and identify the offending element, thereby diagnosing the incongruity responsible for amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in piecemeal literary analysis (Beckett, Sterne) to show that Carroll’s formal notion, when used this way, is informative (helps capture both similarities and differences across comic passages). Use this as an explicit empirical test of theoretical precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer formal definitions for flexibility but beware vagueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal definitions (e.g., violations of norms/expectations) are preferred for being flexible and capable of accounting for a wide range of comic instances, but their generality risks vagueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article defends a formal approach but argues it must be sharpened (via pertinence) to avoid vacuity or shoehorning. Use formal definitions together with contextual constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-determination requires persuasive interpretation (do not adjust context arbitrarily)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining whether a norm is pertinent to a context may require argument and evaluation of interpretations; one cannot simply adjust the relevant context ad hoc to shoehorn an incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bariselli emphasizes that claiming a norm is pertinent must be supported (e.g., in Three Stooges scenes objects are otherwise inanimate, unlike in Beauty and the Beast). Successful appeals to pertinence require convincing interpretative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of non-humorous incongruities (use pertinence to classify surreal/estranging cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some incongruities that meet Carroll’s experiential sufficiency conditions (non-threatening, not problem-solving, etc.) nonetheless do not produce amusement (e.g., certain surrealist artworks); such cases can be classified as non-humorous when the supposedly relevant norms are not pertinent to the artwork’s context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bariselli uses pertinence to show why Miró paintings or Beckett’s Ill Seen Ill Said may be non-comic despite apparent incongruities: the spectator is invited to immerse in an alternate rule-set, making ordinary norms external and non-pertinent.
